The interesting patient at the Schoen-
brunn menagerie, the sick rhinoceros, ap-
pears at length to have recovered from the
severe attack Of influenza under which she
has been suffering. A few days ago she
took her first walk in the open air,
strongly barred Enclosure in the park near
the elephants ground having been assigned
to her. She showed signs of illness during
the latter part Of her sea voyage and her
van from Trieste to Vienna was heated by
sixty hat water tins. Unfortunately on
reaching the CITY, chilly day increased
her cold. and she refused all food. She
was ordered daily five to six quarts Of
camomile tea and several quarts of red
wine. She swallowed this strange diet with
great willingness, and perhaps, preferred
1t to the chopped hay and green food to
which she has now returned. The fear Of
approaching her made the surgeons task
difficult, for even sick rhinoceros is
enormously strong. She Is fine young fe-
male, three and one-half years old, and
was sent to the emperor's menagerie from
the Malay peninsula. Great interest has
been taken In her recovery, among her visi-
tors being the German crown prince. The
treatment employed by the veterinary sur
geon has also been much criticised, but
the result shows it's correctness.

twelve stores here at the beginning of
1902 has reawakened the anti-Ameri-
can agitation. A mass meeting has been
held to appeal to the government to
protect Austrian shoemakers from
American competition.

said he regretted that the commercial
treaty between Austria and the United
States prevented the government from
forbidding the opening of the stores.
but he was convinced that every Vien-
nese would boycott the invaders.


The president of the shoemakers' un-
ion said that the shoe workers intended
to break into the American shops and
smash their contents.


The result Of the agitation Is that all
Vienna is eagerly awaiting the coming
Of the Americans, who say that they
can sell better boots at half the Aus
trian price.

woman 80 years old, residing at 1915 Geary
street, committed suicide last Monday
night by inhaling Illuminating gas. When

house for the purpose of attending night
school she affixed one end of a piece of
rubber tubing to gas fixture, turned the
key, lay down on the bed placed the
other end of the tubing in her mouth and
thus ended her unhappy life.


Her son returned home from school
shortly after o'clock and found her dead.
He raised an alarm and a physician was
hurriedly summoned, but life was extinct,


Mrs Wentworth was divorced several
years ago from a man named Apple and
resumed her maiden name, Wentworth.

spirited, and her son says that she twice

dition delayed the rescue Of the crew of a
large craft. When the distress signals were
displayed and the life-savers got to work a
line was fired over the wreck at the first
shot. But the men on board could not see
it for the darkness and the binding lashing
of the sea. Four lines were sent over be-
fore the connection with the shore was
completed. This experience seems to teach
the value of some form of phosphorescent
line which shall be visible at all hours and
under all circumstances.

A special cable to the New York Jour-
nal and Advertiser from Rome yesterday
says: A terrible African wind swept over
Italy today. All southern and central
Italy was in its baleful grasp. The air,
hot and enervating, was laden with sand
and dust. Since early morning Rome was
enveloped in suffocating cloud of dust,
the red fog or sirocco dust which for CEN
turtles has been the bane and terror Of
countries bordering on the Mediterranean
sea. At Avellino, Naples, Sorrento, Saser-
ia and many other points fell showers OF
what appeared to be dust and ashes.


While the scorching, parching winds blew
the heavens were aflame with angry color,
making spectacle at once awful and ter
ror-inspiring.


The whole OF Sicily was visited by blood
colored rains. At Rome the sky was yell
low; at Naples red.


The inhabitants are terror-stricken. In
Naples every one OF the 800 churches was
packed with frightened and superstitious
people, frantically beseeching the saints for
protection. Some dreadful disaster is
looked for, the red sandstorm, according
to popular belief, always presaging some
mighty tragedy.


PALERMO, Sicily, March 10-The
"bloody rain" is falling all over Sicily. It
is an infrequent phenomenon here, and is
terror-inspiring. The rain drops resemble
coagulated blood They are thick with
blood-red dust, which is probably swept up
from the African deserts and borne hither
on the strong wind now blowing.


Ever since last night red cloud
stretched across the heavens. the sky be-
ing colored a deep red. Storms of this
nature usually last from twenty-four To
forty-eight hours. They have been known
to last for a week.

sonal affection OF his countrymen. They had
watched him daily, appreciated his splendid
character, felt the charm of his personality.

tradition of his virtues. So the whole people
look TO Buffalo and watch the preparations for

exaitation. During the anxious day and night

scene spread before them, and IN Its sadness

ever more calm, gentle resigned and hopeful

on board the steamer Finance, which ar
rived here today from Colon, gives the fol-
lowing account of the capture of Colon by

I'VE were right in the thick of it. Many
of the rife balls whistled over the ship
and while the firing lasted we kept under
cover. The liberals, about 200 in number
came down from the interior by train.
having paid their fares as individuals, and

ernment authorities and soon had control.
They appointed civil officers to run the city.
The United States cruisers Maehias and
Marietta were in the harbor and landed
marines to protect property. When we left
the liberals were still in charge. Great
excitement prevailed among the people on
Sunday morning, November "a, when the
government gunboat Pinzon arrived. Short
II after the gunboat arrived the foreign
warships assembled and boats passed be-
tween them Lengthy signals were also
exchanged between the MachiaS and the
American marines ashore. and an officer
from that vessel landed bearing dispatc ches.
When it was announced that the city would
be bOmbarded people began to leave the
city, and the war vessels and other craft
offered refuge to families, but it was
learned later that the bombardment would
not take place until the foreign consulS
could have opportunity to get their people
out. Just before the Finance left, train
arrived from Panama with 200 marines.
Ahead of the locomotive was an armored
car with two machine guns mounted and
flying the stars and stripes"

The death record of Baltimore that has
held good in the memory of the very Oldest
inhabitant of the city was broken last week
and the seven days just passed stand as
the most terrible in the history of Balti-
more. The total number Of deaths was 451
of which large percentage Is traceable d.
rectly to the awful heat. Seventy-eieht
died from sunstroke and heat prostration.
Heart trouble. superinduced by the heat.
Killed Is. and 134 children died from infan-
tile diarrhoea, disease largely made fatal
by the heat.


Three-quarters of the whole number of
deaths We're among the very young or the
very old, these having the least power of
resistance to the deadly effect of the hot
wave Young babies and aged men and
Women. whose lives under normal condi-
tions might have been preserved, sue
cumbed by the score. One hundred and
ninety children under one year old died
during the week. this number alone being
only five less than the complete record for
the preceding week. The death rate under
these circumstances ascended like a rocket
and reached the alarming figure 1895 for
the whole population. The record is all
the more remarkable because OF the ex-
tremely low rate of the week before, when
there were but 195 deaths reported. -s..s

Cape Town, Oct. 17.-In brisk fight at Twen-

Captain Bellew and four other British were
killed and several others were wounded.


The British having surprised several camps
the Beers are now in the habit of shifting camp
by night. Lately the British columns. after long
night marches. have arrived at their objective
points only to find the Beers gone.


British columns penetrating Orange River Col
ony miles from the railways find fields of maize
or freshly ploughed lands. the Beers making off
at their approach and returning when the col
umns pass on. The herds on the high veldt still
seem to be numerous The Beers are living on
cattle and mealies stored in out of the wav
places


The invaders have reached the sea- COM
mando of FIVE hundred men having penetrated
through the Great Berg River Valley to Hope
field and Saldanha Bay, northwest of Cape
Town


The republicans have secured a number of
recruits and considerable quantities of supplies.
General French is directing operations against
them


saldanha Bay is about sixty miles from Cape
Town. No Boer force has come so near the Cape
Colony capital since the war began.


This inroad is interesting feature Of the con-
fict That 500 Beers should leave the nearest
point the boundary OF the South African Re
public than 500 miles behind them. as the
crow flies and penetrate into and through the
heart of Cape Colony, may indicate only poor
Judgment on the part of the commando leaders,
who are now presumably cut off from all COM
munication with their friends and surrounded
by a hostile population exceeding their own
numbers several thousandfold On the other
hand, It might indicate great disafection toward
the British Crown on the part Of the Cape Colo
nsts along the extended route which this bold 800
followed in order to get so TO Cape Town as
they are now. The fact that Wednesdays fight was
at Piquetberg seems to show that the Beers had
advanced about twenty miles from Saldanha Bay
toward Cape Town TO meet General French's
forces Had the Beers been defeated. there seems
little doubt that the dispatches would have said
To-day's reports may reveal the commando nearer
Cape Town than ever. The raid this little
band of determined men may become famous in
history.

in 1872 when the child was about Eve years

Intense heat prevailed during the great
er part Of the week throughout the CEN

the last three days We're more moderate
Good rains have fallen over large part
of the drought area in the Mississippi and
upper Missouri valleys. but drought con-
ditions have become more serious in the
Ohio Valley and Tennessee, where the
week has been rainless, except in a few
localities. In the Atlantic Coast districts
the weather conditions have been gener-
ally favorable, except over portions of
the Carolinas and Virginia where rain is
now needed The conditions were also
favorable on the Pacific Coast.


Recent rains have improved late corn
iE portions of Nebraska, Kansas. Okla
homa, and Missouri, but the early crop
was practically ruined before the rains
came. In Iowa the crop has sustained less
injury than in the aforementioned
States. and the rainfall has been copious
and well distributed. In the great corn
States east of the Mississippi River, ex-
cept over northern Illinois, drought and
excessive neat have continued with dis
astrous effects upon corn, which is now
in a critical condition. In Michigan and
generally throughout the Middle Allan

Dakota and northern Minnesota the crop
has sustained but little injury from heat.


Oat harvest continues in the more

ture ripening continue from the upper

The condition OF cotton over the great

good growth and clean fields being gen.

In the Ohio Valley and Tennessee to-
bacco continues to suffer from drought
but in Kentucky and Tennessee has with

New England and the Middle and South
Atlantic states the crop has made good
growth. Cutting and curing continue in

There was a desperate and nearly fatal en-
counter in the East Range. a deer run in the
New-York Geological Gardens yesterday be-
tween the Peking Syka deer and keeper
Thomas Quinn, who succored by William
McEnroy another keeper. The deer is called
Boxer and Murderer, which names, the keepers
say, are interchangeable in his case.


The house in the range needed painting and
Assistant Curator Ditmars sent two painters to
do the work. They declined the job unless they
could have couple Of keepers to guard them
from the fierce deer. who lives alone because
he would kill any other of his kind that was
kept with him. Quinn and McEnroy were armed
with clubs and sent TO guard the painters. Sew
eral times Boxer attacked the keepers and was
driven away with the clubs. Finally, while Nc
Enroy was separated from Quinn. the deer made
a desperate rush for the latter running like
whirlwind, with his horns down. Quinn struck
at him with his club. but missed, and the next
instant Boxer knocked him down. Fortu-
nately. the horns did not strike Quinn a Tair
point-on blow. Before he could rise Boxer
at him again. The animal does not strike with
his feet. do American deer, or Quinn might
have been trampled TO death before assistance
could have reached him. Boxer lowered mis-
horns. and struck Quinn the leg, one horn
passing completely through the calf.


Quinn did not shout for help, neither paint





of the house. knew of his danger. He managed

treated for an instant. With lowered horns he
prepared for another attack and this time Quinn
called his mate McEnroy arrived in time to
assist the plucky Quinn to repel the onslaught.
and together they cowed the animal and drove
him to the further end of the range. Quinn's
leg has a serious but not necessarily danger
Gus wound, and he is likely to be unable to
report for duty for some time

tackled. short time ago Mr.. Ditmars was

with fear and panic. 1t seems, however,

Mary, and in doing so gave up her own
life.

The charred remains of the mother and

The original plan of the Cramps, her
builders, was to give the Retvizan a speed
trial later on. the contract requiring that
she make eighteen knots an hour for
twelve hours of consecutive steaming,
but on the run from Sandy Hook
yesterday the battleship made such
speed that Edwin S. Cramp suggested to

only did the Retvizan meet her contract
requirements, but she also broke the
speed record for first-class batteships

she drop below eighteen knots. and for
one hour she made nineteen knots. Her
official time was taken every half hour
during the run, and when figured cut gave
the vessel the average speed of eighteen
and eight-tenths knots. Having satisfied
lilt ttuSSldlS ana Ter DulluerS, the speed
trial planned for tomorrow has been
abandoned. The officers and crew will
spend the day and Sunday sightseeing and
resting up for the test on Monday.


The battleship will then be run over the
Cape Ann course of ten nautical miles,
four times each way, for the purpose of
standardiZing her screws. During the
seventeen hours run from Sandy Hook
the Retvizan averaged an even eighteen
knots an hour, although her official

London, April 23-According to a dispatch
from st. Petersburg to THE Daily Mail" official
information has been received that renewed
military activity is beginning in Manchuria
Chinese troops strongly intrenched at three
points around Moukden. They are armed with
good Mauser rifles, and have thirty Krupp guns
To the eastward of MOukden, Turchausen
there twelve thousand men under the chief
Boxer general Lutanse. To the northwest near
Kulo, there are six thousand Chinese under the
former Governor of Moukden. To the eastward
IN Mongolia and near the In-Shan Mountains
there are nine thousand more under the Chinese
General Schu.


Admiral Alexief has accordingly organized
expedition under General Zerpinsky, consist
ing Of two regiments and five sotnias of Cos
sacks, sixteen guns and body Of volunteers to
operate against the three points mentioned.
The first movement was successfully carried out
in the beginning of April. Kuo. which is $50
kilometres from Moukden. stormed. and
the Ex-Governor of Moukden taken pris-
oner. In this action the Russians had thirteen
men killed and four officers and eighteen men
wounded. The advance toward the Turchausen
position then begun.


Owing to the departure of most of the Russian
troops from Moukden, the latter city has be-
very unsafe. Almost nightly Russian
sentinels are found shot in the back.

quietng and another advance of Russian troops

NEW YORK, March 5.-A sixteen-year-
old actress whose stage name was Mamie
Cirelli, was shot and killed early this morn
ing by her jealous lover, Antonio Trioio,
twenty years old. The murder was COM
mitted at the corner of Mulberry and Bay
ard streets. TYiolo was arrested. The
dead girl and her mother, Santina Magav-
ero, also an actress. have been travelling
about the country, giving performances in
small concert halls and other resorts fire.
quented by Italians.


About week ago they began an engage
ment al the Villa Umbert, in Mulberry
street. They had appeared at this place
on several other occasions, and it was here
that Triolo met the girl.


Shortly after 1 o'clock this morning. with
her mother and Gugivelino Sorentino, a
friend of the mother the girl left the hall
and walked down Mulberry street. They
had reached the northeast corner of Bay
ard street when Triolo. who had evidently
been waiting in a doorway, was seen walk
ing rapidly toward them. When he was
within a few feet of the trio he drew a
revolver, and pointing it at the girl emptied
the five chambers in quick succession. Two
of the bullets took effect, either one being
sufficient to cause death. Triolo ran away,
but was caught by policeman. He said
the girl had preferred other men to him
and that he could not live without her.

USHERlNG IN THE NEW CENTURY.


The effect of New-York City's noisy welcome TO
the new century as heard at a country place the
Sound. twelve miles from the city, was remarkably
impressive. The midnight pandemonium of scream
ing steam whistles changing BELLS countless horns
and all the general uproar resolved itself into
high throbbing musical note that seemed to fill the
world just as if mighty tuning fork had struck
the universe and ELECTED tone note of jubilation
that prolonged itself Indefinitely through space
and moonlit atmosphere, While along the horizon
the far off electric lights shot up in rays and
pulsated like an aurora borealis. From the water.
from the land came the musical tone note, and,
like the deep bass in overture, the continuous
roar of the cannon made its accompaniment.


II is only in the country and the water that
really gets the impressive effect OF such a
celebration In the city the immediate local noises
quite drown the nobler sounds Half dozen penny
trumpets blown by the lusty lungs of enthusiastic
youngsters will overpower the finest chimes, and
nearby firecrackers eclipse the distant cannon
laundering from the fortiications. but out In the
quiet country and contrasted with the stiffness of
sleeping and forest the effect OF the musical
rushing of combined sounds coming suddenly
after the intense stiffness of waiting is wonderfully
solemn, especially think OF what t heralds-
a century for country, with all its wonder
full developments and changes!

The assurances which Mr.. Infante, Chill

lations between Chile and Argentina are
based upon official dispatches received by
Mr.. Infante from his government. 1t ap-
pears that Chile has been sending parties
of civil engineers into the mountains lying
between Chile and Argentina with view
to marking boundary line between the
two countries. This action excited COM
plant from critics hostile to Chile, who
asserted that she was quietly building mil
itary roads to command the passes between
the two countries. The Argentine govern
ment finally took cognizance of these crit
icisms. and in a friendly spirit made in
quiry of Chile as to whether these were
military roads. The explanation was at
once given that the roads were solely for
the engineering parties marking the boun-
dairy. This has allayed the apparent fric-
tion, and has permitted the Chilean author
tiles to give positive official assurances
that the entire affair will be settled, and
that the present relations between Chile
and Argentina are now of the most friend
ly character.

FROM the Ladies Home journal.


In the Cincinnati Zoo dwelt two giraffes
Giraffes are not noted for their affection,
yet these two exhibited every evidence of
true devotion to each other The male
never seemed to tire Of caressng the long,
slender neck of his partner and, what was
most unusual, would frequently leave for
her the softest and choicest bits of food
On one occasion when she was removed
from the pen for a short time and quar-
tered near by, he seemed to find consola-
tion in some bits Of cloth that had been
used to bind her throat; always lying down
beside them, no matter where they hap
pened to be placed. And during this tenn
porary separation the two would spend
hours gazing longingly at each other across
the space that divided them. When they
were again united they made manifest
their supreme happiness by frolicking
about like frisky colts. blissfully unmind-
full Of the fact that such behavior was
anything but picturesque in creatures Of
their build.
headline: Love Story of Two Giraffes.

violence. Finally, however. they became
concerned for the safety Of the prisoners
whom they were holding for the county
authorities. They notified the warden of
the county Jail and quarters were at once

NEW YORK. Nov. 4.-Nothing of great
significance and very little of interest re-
suited from today's transactions in the
stock market The market opened with
none of the buoyancy which had charac-
terized the trading in the closing dealings
on Saturday, and, indeed, price changes
were limited and irregular, with business
in light volume. Subsequent movements
were more than ordinarily irregular.


After the opening there was quite a
pronounced rise in Union Pacific and st.
Paul, the movement in question extending
to the remainder of the list in slight
degree but upon its elimination the whole
market subsided into irregularity. A few
stocks showed distinct and effective pres
sure, noteworthy examples being Peoples
Gas and Sugar Refining. and their course
was not without effect upon the rest of
the market The additional engagements
of gold for export were further obstacle
to speculative activity, as it was feared
that the outflow would soon be reflected
in the money market, and, indeed, today's
rates were higher. Sterling exchange was
a shade easier A number of interesting
returns of railway traffic were submitted.


Interest again centred almost wholly
around the expected settlement of the
Northern Pacific situation. Further def
mite information was. however not forth
coming. The early quotations showed
that the London market had refused to
accept the advances made in the local
dealings on Saturday, and declines ex-
tending from 4 to Il point below parity
with our closing prices were shown. For
eign houses sold about twenty thousand
shares of stocks here within the course
of the morning.


Firm features of the railway list were
AtchisCn common. the Southern Railway
shares, and st. Louis and San Francisco.
Otherwise, however, the market for rail-
way stocks had an irregular and general
ly reactionary tendency.


The local traction shares We're wanting
in strength. while Consolidated Gas con-
tinued heavy. The copper stocks were
comparatively dull. The United States
Steel stocks. while active. did not retain
the buoyancy they displayed in Satur-
days closing dealings

LONDON, January 24.-The British Medi-
cal Journal publishes an authoritative ac-
count Of the last illness Of Queen Victoria
It says the queens health, for year, had
been falling, with symptoms mainly of a
dyspeptic kind, accompanied by impaired
nutrition and periods Of insomnia, and later
there were slight, transitory attacks Of
aphasia- In the general arterial system
there were remarkably few signs Of age.


After alluding to the symptoms of SOM
nolence increasing the cerebral exhaustion
which her majesty's strong will enabled her
to hide from momentary visitors, the Medi-
cal Journal confirms the Associated Press
Information saying that Thursday her men,
tai confusion was more marked and a
slight fluttering was observed In the right
side of her face.


Thence forward aphasia and facial
paralysis became permanent. It is import
ant to note, the Medical Journal adds, that
Notwithstanding the great bodily weakness
and cerebral exhaustion. the hearts action
was steadily maintained to the last. The
pulse was always regular and the tempera-
ture normal. In the last few hours paraly-
sis of the pulmonary nerves set in.


Beyond a slight facial fluttering there
never was any motor paralysis,

Mountain eagles are reported to be
swarming on the Tomichi, near Gunni-
son, feasting on the thousands of rab-
bits driven into the valley by the snow in
the mountains and foothills. The ranch
men fear that the ravenous hunger Of the
eagles will tempt them to attack human
beings.


One of the eagles met its match a few
days ago. Ferrets have been brought into
the valley to kill rabbits. This particular
eagle swooped down upon ferret The
ferret caught the eagle by the throat and
the bird few far into the air. Only a
few moments elapsed when the eagle came
tumbling down. The ranchman who had
watched the mid-air battle ran over to
the fallen bird and found it dead. The
ferret had bitten through the throat and
was still clinging to the bird.


Tom Holland, superintendent of fish
cries, said the other night that the eagles
were providing good sport for ranchmen,
and that several large ones had been
brought down with guns in the hands of
ranchmen in the valley.

Port Elizabeth, Feb. 21.-The following
proclamation has been issued by President
Steyn and General De Wet:


Be it known TO all men that the war, which
has been forced on the Transyaal republics
by the British government, still RACES over
South Africa; that all the customs of civilized
warfare and also the conventions Of Geneva
and The Hague are not observed by the
enemy, who have not scrupled, contrary to
the Geneva convention, to capture doctors and
prevent our wounded from getting medical
assistance; that they have seized ambulance
material appertaining thereto; that they have
not hesitated to have recourse TO primitive
rules of warfare, contrary to the solemn
agreement of The Hague; TO arrest neutrals
and deport them, and to send out marauding
bands TO plunder. burn and damage burghers'
private property; that they have armed
Kafirs and natives and used them against
us in the war; that they have been con-
tinually capturing women and children and
old and sickly men and that there have been
many deaths among the women because the
so-called Christian enemy had no consiGera-
tion for women on a sckbed, or whose state
of health should have protected them against
rough treatment


Honorable women and tender children have
not only been treated roughly, but have been
insulted by soldiers. by order of their officers.
Moreover old mothers and women have been
assaulted, even wives and children, and the
property OF prisoners of war even killed
burghers, has not been respected.


In many instances the mother and father
have been taken. the house has been left un-
protected and all have been left to their fate

Sweeping away on its noiseless wings,
The finished century takes its flight,
Yielding unchallenged to yon faint light
That newly a century's promise brings.
What can the oncoming swift years hold
More than the wonders that mark today?
Is not the tale Of the ages told?
What can the Twentieth Century say?
To minds that shrink at the muster roll,
OF wonders that dazzle the thought Of man;
The worlds full conQuest-from pole to pole
Almost! When triumphs the hopeful plan.
The friendlier stars in their shining scroll,
Reveal the laws of their power TO shine;
Telling to eyes that read the whole
The hand that made is the hand Divine"
Let the faulty past with its failings, go.
Gather its blessings for new surprise;
Passing. In faith. from the things we know
To worthier deeds under fairer skies.
What shall we render of joyful praise
For all the good in the worlds great hand?
Service and cheer shall employ the days
And kindness honor the great command.
Master and man in the coming years
Each for the other a thought shall hold,
Cheerfuly serving with mutual cares,
Winning and spending the precious gold.
Each for the other, the great world through;
What will 1t do for the days that come?
Peace and truth shall all wrong undo,
And the century prove the millennium!

Board CCongregationaD for about nineteen years.


About thirteen years ago, after locust famine,
Mrs. Shepherd. sorely perplexed to know how to
bring relief the many hundreds of suffering
people. hit upon plan to adapt the wonderful
drawn work of Persia and the exquisite needle lace
of Armenia to the modern Western market.
Models obtained from Persia and Smyrna,
and after much study patterns were selected which
were adapted especially to handkerchiefs. doies.
centre pieces luncheon cloths etc. Women were
trained to do the work in the most exquisite man.
ner. the result being a refinement of the ancient
Oriental needle arts. For the foundation the
choicest linens of Europe and Asia were used
Gradually other materials and styles of work were
added and the three hundred picked women
of Aintab make not only all sorts Of linen pieces
used in the household decorating them with Per
sian drawn work and Armenian needle lace, but
they also produce beautiful scarfs for bureau,
dressing table. buffet and the like, of fine twned
linens from Trebizond silk crepe made in hand
looms in Antioch. gauze from Brusa, and other
fabrics for which the East is famous. These are
ornamented with silk and gold work. and in many
cases the ends are finished with the thread and
needle lace flowers much used In adorning the
costumes of the Moslem women

the women of Marash. another town of Central

stitch embroidery, which they put on hand loom
cottons 10 sofa pillows, couch covers. porteres and

into trouble yesterday The sight of his
master shaving himself was too much for

badly.

ing implements yesterday Jerry followed
him and was an interested spectator Of the
operation. After the sergeant had finished
he left the room for moment and did not
put his razor away. That was golden
opportunity for Jerry.

key and went to him. Jerry was sitting
on the table with the razor in his paw and
the blood flowing from wound in his neck

Some months ago Tony Holland and his
wife. highly respected citizens Of Talla-
hatchie county. Miss. left their little farm
home to take stroll in the woods. The
old gentleman carried along his rifle. in
the hope of getting a shot at a squirrel
perhaps turkey. Shortly after they
went away two reports of the rifle were
heard. but nothing was thought about it
until nearly night, when some members
of the family; becoming uneasy at their
long stay. walked down the path in the
direction they had gone, and soon came
upon them lying on the ground dead. The
woman had been shot through and through
from the back. and lay face down in the
path. The old gentleman was a few feet
from her with the whole top of his head
blown off They were very devoted cou-
pie. and the supposition was that the gun
had been accidentally discharged, killing
the wife. and that In his despair the hus-
band took his own life.


The question then was as to which OF
the two had died first, the disposition of the
estate depending on that one point. Ann
Duncan claimed the property, as heir to
her brother. Mr.. Holland, on the ground
that he had done the killing, and that. as
a matter of course, he had killed his wife
first. The court below took her view OF
the matter and awarded her the estate
The near relatives of Mrs. Holland took
an appeal to the supreme court of Miss:s-
sippi. claiming she had died last where
fore they should inherit the property The
vestigation into the killing of the old con-
pie. and found that in fact the woman
had died last. though shot first Her body
was warm when found, and the body of her
husband was cold, showing conclusveIy in
the opinion of the court, that she had lived
some four or five hours longer than her
husband did, and that her immediate rela-
tives should inherit the estate.
